hook: Drive a lab cart by setting only its position, velocity or acceleration, and watch all three motion graphs draw at once. Then race a ghost of your best run on ten target graphs.
outcome: Read and make position, velocity and acceleration graphs, and see that each graph is the slope of the one above it and the area under the one below it
sources: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, chapter 3, Motion Along a Straight Line (displacement, velocity, acceleration, slopes and areas of motion graphs, constant-acceleration equations): https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/3-introduction
OpenStax, Physics (high school), chapter 2, Motion in One Dimension: https://openstax.org/books/physics/pages/2-introduction
OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, section 5.3, Newton's Second Law (the F = m a force readout): https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/5-3-newtons-second-law

Misconceptions targeted: McDermott, Rosenquist and van Zee, Student difficulties in connecting graphs and physics, American Journal of Physics 55, 503 (1987); Beichner, Testing student interpretation of kinematics graphs, American Journal of Physics 62, 750 (1994)
Target motions are original, built from piecewise definitions and integrated exactly (end positions checked)
Cart, track, sensor, graphs, thumbnails and arrows drawn in code; sounds generated in the browser
Background image generated on this PC with FLUX.1-schnell (Apache 2.0), no people
Narration generated with Qwen3-TTS (Apache 2.0), cloning a Google Gemini text-to-speech voice
